1. Belief update: M18 is currently the most plausible mechanism, followed by M11, M14, and M20. M12 is also somewhat plausible but less likely.
2. Hypothesis discrimination: The critical difference between the top model (M18) and the runner-up cluster (M14, M11, M20) is the kinetic order of the deactivation step. M18 involves bimolecular deactivation of the catalyst-substrate complex (2catS => inactive), making the deactivation rate second-order with respect to [catS]. In contrast, M14 involves unimolecular deactivation (catS => inactive), which is first-order in [catS].
3. Discriminative experiment design: To strongly differentiate between first-order and second-order deactivation in [catS], we should run an experiment with the maximum allowable catalyst concentration (cat = 0.2) and a saturating substrate concentration (S = 3.0). This will maximize the concentration of the catS complex.
4. Contrastive prediction:
- For M18 (2catS => inactive), the deactivation rate scales with the square of [catS]. Doubling the catalyst concentration (compared to the previous run) will quadruple the deactivation rate but only double the initial product formation rate. This will cause the reaction to halt disproportionately early, yielding a lower turnover number (TON) per catalyst.
- For M14 (catS => inactive), the deactivation rate is first-order in [catS]. Doubling the catalyst will double both the product formation rate and the deactivation rate, resulting in roughly the same final fractional conversion (constant TON).
- For M11 (S+cat => inactive), deactivation depends on free [cat]. Under saturating substrate conditions, most of the catalyst is tied up as catS, which protects it from deactivation initially. The reaction will only plateau later as S is depleted and free [cat] increases.
- For M12 (P+cat => inactive), the reaction will not experience early deactivation but will instead slow down progressively as product accumulates.
</hypothesis>
